name: Adam Smith
kicker: Scottish economist · Father of modern free-market capitalism
briefing: Adam Smith was a Scottish professor who wondered why a factory full of workers each doing one small job could make thousands of pins a day, while one worker alone could barely make twenty. In 1776 he published _The Wealth of Nations_, arguing that people chasing their own self-interest in a free market often help everyone else too, as if guided by an “invisible hand.” He is now called the father of modern economics.

sample.note: 10 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 8 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This thinker’s mentor at the University of Glasgow was the philosopher Francis Hutcheson, whose ideas shaped this man’s own views on morality. This man’s theory that a good’s worth comes from the labor used to make it was later expanded by Karl Marx, even though Marx used it to attack the economic system this man defended.
tossups.r: This man explained how specializing in small, repeated tasks let workers make far more pins in a day than if each worker made a whole pin alone. For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man delivered unpublished lecture series titled _Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres_ and _Lectures on Jurisprudence_ while he held a chair at the University of Glasgow. In his first book, this man argued that people behave morally to win the approval of an imagined “impartial spectator.”
tossups.r: That book, _The Theory of Moral Sentiments_, came years before his most famous work. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist who later described a self-regulating free market as guided by an “invisible hand.”

tossups.p: This man criticized the mercantilist policies of French minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert [“kohl-BEHR”], arguing that a nation’s wealth is not just the gold and silver it hoards. This man’s own economic ideas were later built on by David Ricardo, who used them to develop the theory of comparative advantage.
tossups.r: This man used the example of a butcher, a brewer, and a baker to argue that self-interest, not kindness, is what gets you your dinner. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist and author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man once asked what makes a diamond so expensive while water, which is far more useful, costs so little, a puzzle he framed by separating “value in use” from “value in exchange.” Scholars still debate a famous puzzle in economic philosophy, named for this thinker, about how his praise of sympathy fits with his praise of self-interest.
tossups.r: He explained that specialized workers in a pin factory could produce far more than the same workers each making whole pins alone. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist who wrote about the “division of labor.”

tossups.p: This man argued that the rich should be taxed more than just in proportion to their income, not less. He once wrote that an important question of moral philosophy is “wherein does virtue consist?”, a question he explored years before writing his most famous book.
tossups.r: That later book argued that free markets often work best when government mostly stays out of the way, an idea called laissez-faire [“less-ay FAIR”]. For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man’s close friendship with fellow Scottish philosopher David Hume lasted from their years together in Edinburgh until Hume’s death. This man’s first book argued that people judge right and wrong by imagining how an outside observer would react.
tossups.r: That book, _The Theory of Moral Sentiments_, came before the work that made him famous. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist whose later book described self-interested trade as guided by an “invisible hand.”

tossups.p: This man’s full title for his most famous book is _An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations_. In that 1776 book, this man rejected mercantilism, the idea that nations should hoard gold and restrict trade.
tossups.r: He explained that a pin factory could make far more pins per day once the work was split into small, specialized steps. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist who described free markets as guided by an “invisible hand.”

tossups.p: This man taught Logic and then Moral Philosophy as a professor at the University of Glasgow before tutoring a young duke in France and Switzerland. His first major book, _The Theory of Moral Sentiments_, studied sympathy as the basis of human morality.
tossups.r: His far more famous second book argued that a butcher, a brewer, and a baker serve you dinner out of self-interest, not kindness. For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man spent years in France observing the Physiocrats before returning to Scotland to keep writing his most famous book. He argued that splitting work into small, repeated steps, which he illustrated with a pin factory, could multiply how much a group of workers produces.
tossups.r: This economist is best known for arguing that people pursuing their own self-interest in a free market often benefit society as a whole, as if guided by an “invisible hand.” For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man’s theory of value, which said that the price of a good reflects the labor that went into making it, influenced later economists including Karl Marx and David Ricardo, who took his ideas in very different directions. His 1759 book studied sympathy and an “impartial spectator.”
tossups.r: His far more famous 1776 book rejected mercantilism and praised free trade, self-interest, and the division of labor. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist and author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man argued that a free market works like an “invisible hand,” guiding people who are only trying to help themselves into also helping society as a whole. He used the example of a pin factory to show how splitting work into small, specialized tasks raises production.
tossups.r: This economist criticized mercantilism and praised free trade and self-interest, as in his example of the butcher, the brewer, and the baker. For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man wrote that people judge their own and others’ behavior through the eyes of an imagined “impartial spectator” in his book _The Theory of Moral Sentiments_. He had earlier studied under the philosopher Francis Hutcheson at the University of Glasgow.
tossups.r: This man’s far more famous book described free markets as guided by an “invisible hand” and used a pin factory to explain the division of labor. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist, the author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man’s idea that a good’s value comes from the labor that produced it was later used by Karl Marx to criticize the very economic system this man championed. This man also described an “impartial spectator” whose imagined approval guides moral behavior.
tossups.r: This economist is best remembered for describing free markets as guided by an “invisible hand” in his 1776 book. For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

tossups.p: This man rejected mercantilism, arguing that a nation grows wealthy through trade and productive labor rather than by hoarding gold and silver. He illustrated the benefits of the “division of labor” using the example of workers in a pin factory.
tossups.r: This economist used the example of a butcher, a brewer, and a baker to argue that self-interest, not kindness, puts food on your table. For 10 points, name this Scottish author of _The Wealth of Nations_, who described free markets as guided by an “invisible hand.”

tossups.p: This man’s first book, _The Theory of Moral Sentiments_, argued that sympathy, not pure self-interest, is the foundation of human morality. He later studied how splitting tasks among workers in a pin factory could multiply their output.
tossups.r: This man’s most famous book praised free trade, criticized mercantilism, and described self-interested exchange as guided by an “invisible hand.” For 10 points, name this Scottish economist and author of _The Wealth of Nations_.

clues.t: Scottish economist and philosopher, often called the father of modern economics
Wrote _The Wealth of Nations_ (1776), the book that helped found modern economics
Famous for the “invisible hand,” the idea that a free market can regulate itself
Used a pin factory to show the benefits of splitting work into small, specialized tasks (“division of labor”)
Also wrote _The Theory of Moral Sentiments_, an earlier book about sympathy and morality
Argued that people acting in their own self-interest can still end up benefiting society as a whole
Used the butcher, the brewer, and the baker as an example: self-interest, not kindness, gets you your dinner
Criticized mercantilism, the idea that a nation should hoard gold and silver and restrict trade
Supported laissez-faire [“less-ay FAIR”] economics: keeping government mostly out of free markets
_The Wealth of Nations_’s full title is _An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations_
Taught Logic and then Moral Philosophy as a professor at the University of Glasgow
Close friend of fellow Scottish philosopher David Hume; the two were linked to Edinburgh
Posed the “diamond-water paradox” (useful water is cheap, but diamonds are costly), separating value in use from value in exchange
His labor theory of value, that a good’s worth comes from the work that made it, was later expanded by Karl Marx
His ideas were built on by David Ricardo, who developed the theory of comparative advantage
Studied under Francis Hutcheson at Glasgow, a mentor who shaped this man’s own moral philosophy
Also delivered the lecture series _Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres_ and _Lectures on Jurisprudence_
_The Theory of Moral Sentiments_ introduced the “impartial spectator,” an imagined observer whose approval guides moral behavior
Criticized French minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert’s mercantilist policies as an example of bad economics
A famous puzzle in economic philosophy, named for this thinker, asks how his praise of sympathy in one book fits with his praise of self-interest in another
Argued that the rich should be taxed more than just in proportion to their income, not less
Asked what he called an important question of moral philosophy: “wherein does virtue consist?”
Born in 1723 in Kirkcaldy [“kur-KAW-dee”], a small Scottish port town

trap.title: Smith or Marx?
trap.body: Adam Smith helped develop the labor theory of value, the idea that a good’s worth comes from the work that made it, almost a century before Karl Marx used that same idea to criticize capitalism. A clue about “labor theory of value” or about explaining prices through labor could be building toward either economist.
trap.fix: Smith is the 18th-century Scot who defended free markets and self-interest; Marx is the 19th-century German who used economics to argue capitalism exploits workers. If the clue says “pin factory,” “division of labor,” “butcher, brewer, and baker,” “invisible hand,” or “1776,” it is Smith.
